title: Rospotrebnadzor inspection: a checklist for the day before the visit
excerpt: Employee medical records, the production-control program, pest-control contracts, waste-removal documents, and journals for the past 12 months. What to prepare in one day—and what not to do before an inspection.

body.text: A planned inspection is scheduled 20 working days in advance; an unscheduled one may sometimes come with just a day’s notice. If the inspector arrives tomorrow, here is what to prepare.

items: Medical records for every employee on shift: valid and showing fluorography results.
The current production-control program, approved by the manager.
The pest-control and disinfection contract, plus the latest service reports.
The contract for food-waste removal and used cooking-oil disposal.
The HACCP plan, if your facility uses one.

body.text: This is what the inspector will focus on. Gather the hygiene, reject-product, temperature, incoming-raw-material, cleaning, and disinfectant journals as PDFs in one folder. In WeSetup, this takes one click: ‘Export for period.’

body.title: Check the signatures
body.text: If the head chef was on leave, the deputy should have signed on their behalf. A blank field marked with a dash may lead to a formal notice.

items: Check that cutting boards and knives are labeled, with a separate color for each product group.
Check expiry dates in the refrigerator: anything without a label or with a smeared date must be discarded.
The refrigerator temperatures must match the journal for the latest shift.
Check work surfaces: make sure no cleaning residue remains and handles are not greasy.

body.text: Do not fill in journals retroactively. Inspectors can spot this from handwriting, ink patterns, and the sequence of dates. It is better to show a missed entry and explain why than to be caught falsifying records—which carries a greater penalty.
